intro/hello: Welcome to training, the part of deep learning that takes most of the actual time.
intro/have: You already have the ingredients: an architecture, prepared data, a starting point for the weights, a loss, and backprop for its gradient.
intro/tend: But a training run is less like running a program, and more like tending an experiment.
intro/check: Before it starts, you check the gradients, and the untrained network.
intro/watch: While it runs, you watch the curves, for a bad learning rate or for overfitting.
intro/update: You pick a smarter update rule, and you lower the learning rate as you go.
intro/search: You search for good settings of the knobs. And at the end, you average several models.
intro/go: Let us take them in order, starting where the bugs hide: the gradient.
gradcheck/bug: Backprop code is easy to get subtly wrong: a missing transpose, a lost factor of two, a flipped sign.
gradcheck/hide: And a buggy gradient often still lowers the loss a little, so the bug can hide for a long time.
gradcheck/defense: The defense is a gradient check: compute the gradient a second, slow but nearly foolproof way, and compare.
gradcheck/nudge: That second way is the definition of the derivative: nudge one parameter, and see how much the loss moves.
gradcheck/both: Nudge it up by a tiny step h, and evaluate the loss. Nudge it down by h, and evaluate again.
gradcheck/rise: Rise over run is the slope of the line through those two points. As h shrinks, the line hugs the curve, and its slope becomes the derivative.
gradcheck/one: Why nudge both ways? Because the one-sided version is off by an amount proportional to h.
gradcheck/bend: Near any point, a smooth curve bends like a parabola. Stepping both ways, that bend cancels out.
gradcheck/table: Shrink h a hundredfold, and the one-sided error shrinks a hundredfold. The centered one shrinks ten thousandfold: it goes like h squared.
gradcheck/cost: It costs two loss evaluations per parameter: far too slow for training, but fine for a check.
relerr/two: Now we have two gradients, numerical and analytic. How do we compare them?
relerr/plain: Not by their plain difference. A gap of ten to the minus four is a one percent disagreement between gradients near a hundredth, and nothing at all between gradients in the thousands.
relerr/rel: So divide by the larger of the two: that is the relative error. Then report the worst entry.
relerr/thumbs: Rules of thumb: above ten to the minus two, the gradient is probably wrong, and down to ten to the minus four, uncomfortable. Below ten to the minus seven, be happy.
relerr/thumbs2: In between is fine for functions with kinks, like ray-loo, but too high for smooth ones.
relerr/precision: Three traps make a correct gradient look wrong. First, precision: in single precision, a correct check can be off by a percent. Use double.
relerr/hstep: Second, the step h. Too large, and the line is a poor stand-in for the curve. Too small, and subtracting two nearly equal numbers wipes out their digits.
relerr/sweet: In double precision, the sweet spot is around ten to the minus six to ten to the minus five.
relerr/kink: Third, kinks. Ray-loo, hinges and max pooling have corners where the slope jumps. If the two nudges straddle one, the check fails, though backprop is right.
relerr/habits: So check on two or three examples, with regularization and dropout off. Train briefly first, and test a few entries of every parameter array.
sanity/three: Before a long run, three quick sanity checks, each one catching a whole family of bugs.
sanity/uniform: One: is the starting loss right? With small random weights, all scores are near zero, so every class gets the same probability: one in ten, for see-far ten.
sanity/ln: The softmax loss is minus the log of that, so it should start near two point three oh two. For the SVM, nine wrong classes each miss the margin by one: nine.
sanity/off: If you see zero point five, or forty, something is off, often weights that start too large.
sanity/reg: Two: turn the regularization way up. The loss should rise. If not, the penalty never reached the loss.
sanity/tiny: Three, the most telling: take twenty examples, turn regularization off, and train.
sanity/memo: A working network easily memorizes twenty points: the loss falls to nearly zero, and training accuracy hits a hundred percent.
sanity/stall: With even a little regularization, it can no longer memorize them.
sanity/converse: Passing this check proves little, but failing it proves a bug. Do not move on until it passes.
losscurve/watch: Once the checks pass, train, and watch. Plot against epochs, full passes over the training set, so the axis means the same whatever the batch size.
losscurve/four: Here are four copies of one network on the spiral data, differing only in their learning rate.
losscurve/low: A low rate improves slowly, almost in a straight line.
losscurve/good: A good rate drops quickly, and keeps improving.
losscurve/high: A high rate drops fast, then stalls at a worse level, bouncing: every step overshoots the narrow parts of the landscape.
losscurve/vhigh: A very high rate makes the loss climb, often to infinity, or to not a number.
losscurve/wiggle: The wiggle from batch to batch reflects the batch size: tiny batches are noisy, and the full dataset is smooth.
losscurve/plateau: A long plateau, then a sudden drop, usually means a bad initialization.
losscurve/logscale: Some people plot the loss on a log scale, where roughly exponential progress looks closer to a straight line.
gap/second: The second plot is accuracy, on the training set and on a validation set, every epoch or so.
gap/task: This network separates two classes along a wavy border, from sixty training points, one in ten of them mislabeled.
gap/over: Training accuracy reaches a hundred percent, as the regions contort around every point. Validation stalls near seventy six.
gap/gapmeans: That gap is overfitting: the network memorized, instead of learning the pattern.
gap/fix: Cure it with more regularization, or more data. Here a stronger penalty smooths the regions, and validation rises to eighty five.
gap/lin: A linear model shows the opposite: no gap, but both stuck near seventy eight. It lacks capacity, so make it bigger.
gap/ratio: Also track each update's size relative to the weights it changes. It should be near a thousandth. In our runs, the low rate sat ten times below that, and the high ones ten times above.
gap/hist: Histograms of each layer's activations reveal a bad initialization. With tan h, you want a spread from minus one to one, not a spike at zero, or piles at the ends.
gap/filt: And for images, view the first layer's weights as pictures: noisy speckles are a warning, smooth and varied filters a good sign.
momentum/what: Backprop gives the gradient. The update rule decides what to do with it.
momentum/sgd: Vanilla gradient descent steps straight down the slope: the weights, minus the learning rate times the gradient.
momentum/zig: In a long, narrow valley, a very common shape, the slope points mostly across the valley, not along it. So it zigzags between the walls, and creeps along the floor.
momentum/ball: Momentum borrows from physics: the parameters are a ball rolling on the landscape. The gradient is a force that changes its velocity, and the velocity moves it.
momentum/cancel: Pushes from the two walls alternate and cancel, while the steady push along the floor adds up, so the ball gains speed where it matters.
momentum/mu: Mu acts like friction, shrinking the old velocity every step. A common choice is zero point nine, which lets the steps grow up to ten times larger.
momentum/overshoot: But a rolling ball also overshoots, and has to swing back.
momentum/nesterov: Nesterov's twist: momentum alone will carry the ball by mu times v anyway, so measure the gradient there, at the look-ahead point.
momentum/ahead: If the ball is about to overshoot, that gradient already says so, and it brakes in time. It consistently works a little better.
adaptive/one: So far, every parameter shares one learning rate. Adaptive methods give each parameter its own step size, from the history of its gradients.
adaptive/ada: Adagrad keeps a running sum of each parameter's squared gradients, the cache, and divides every step by its square root.
adaptive/norm: That normalizes each gradient by its typical size, so every parameter moves by roughly the learning rate, steep or shallow.
adaptive/valley: In the valley, the steep direction is tamed, and the shallow one sped up: no more zigzag.
adaptive/decay: The catch: the sum only grows, so the steps keep shrinking, and learning stops too early.
adaptive/rms: RMSprop, from a lecture slide by Geoff Hinton, swaps the sum for a moving average, so the step size can adapt up as well as down.
adaptive/adam: Adam combines both ideas: a moving average of the gradient, like momentum, divided by the root of a moving average of its square, like RMSprop.
adaptive/bias: Both averages start at zero, so early on they are too small. Dividing by one minus beta to the t corrects that.
adaptive/defaults: With betas of zero point nine and zero point nine nine nine, Adam is the usual default.
adaptive/saddle: Adaptive steps shine on a saddle, a ridge falling away on both sides. Everyone starts just off its top, where the sideways gradient is tiny.
adaptive/escape: SGD and momentum barely move. Adagrad, RMSprop and Adam divide that tiny gradient by its own size, and escape quickly.
anneal/bounce: With a constant learning rate, noisy mini-batch gradients keep kicking the parameters out of the narrow bottom.
anneal/floor: So the loss flattens out at a noise floor.
anneal/lower: The fix: lower the learning rate as training goes on, so the parameters can settle.
anneal/step: Step decay halves it every so often: here, every hundred and fifty steps.
anneal/exp: Exponential decay shrinks it by the same factor every step.
anneal/inv: One over t decay shrinks it fast at first, then ever more slowly.
anneal/settle: Each decaying schedule keeps settling, long after the constant rate has stalled.
anneal/timing: But decay too fast, and the system cools before it reaches the bottom.
anneal/practice: Step decay is the most common. A good habit: halve the rate whenever the validation error stops improving.
newton/first: All of these are first-order methods: they use only the slope. Second-order methods also use the curvature, how fast the slope itself changes.
newton/hess: In many dimensions, that is the Hessian, the grid of all second derivatives.
newton/fit: Newton's method fits a bowl at the current point, and jumps to its bottom. On the long valley, it arrives in one step, with no learning rate at all.
newton/size: So why not use it? A million parameters means a Hessian of a million squared entries: three thousand seven hundred and twenty five gigabytes.
newton/saddle: And Newton is drawn to any flat point. On the saddle, it walks straight to the top of the ridge, and stays.
newton/lbfgs: L-BFGS approximates the Hessian from recent gradients, but it needs the full training set at once: mini-batch noise breaks it.
newton/rec: So use Adam by default, try SGD with Nesterov momentum, and either way, decay the learning rate.
search/knobs: Some knobs training cannot set: above all, the learning rate, its decay, and the regularization strength.
search/val: Tune them on one decent validation set, and automate it: workers sample settings, train, and save each result to disk.
search/log: Search on a log scale. Adding zero point zero one to a rate of zero point zero zero one changes everything. Adding it to ten changes nothing.
search/exp: So sample the exponent uniformly. Knobs like dropout stay linear.
search/grid: And prefer random search to a grid, because usually only a few knobs really matter.
search/waste: A three by three grid tests just three learning rates, three times each, and here, none is near the peak.
search/random: Nine random trials test nine different rates, far more likely to hit the narrow good region.
search/border: Watch the borders: if the best result sits at an edge of the range, widen it.
search/coarse: Go from coarse to fine: wide ranges and one epoch per trial first, then narrower ranges, and about five epochs.
search/fine: Then a fine search with many epochs. Bayesian methods pick trials more cleverly, but a well ranged random search is hard to beat.
ensembles/trick: One last trick buys a few extra percent: train several models, and average their predictions.
ensembles/why: Each model makes its own mistakes, and averaged, they partly cancel. The more the models differ, the bigger the gain.
ensembles/members: Members can be copies with new random starts, the top models of your search, or snapshots of one long run.
ensembles/avgw: Cheapest of all: a running average of the weights, used at test time. It almost always buys a percent or two.
ensembles/bowl: Late in training, the weights jitter around the bottom of a bowl, and their average sits closer to it than any snapshot.
ensembles/cost: The catch is the cost at test time, but an ensemble can be distilled back into one model, trained to match its probabilities.
closing/recap: That is the whole training checklist.
closing/c1: Check gradients numerically, in double precision, on a few examples.
closing/c2: Check the starting loss, and memorize a tiny subset.
closing/c3: Watch the loss curve, and the gap between training and validation.
closing/c4: Update with Adam or Nesterov momentum, and decay the rate.
closing/c6: Search at random, on log scales, coarse to fine. And ensemble at the end.
closing/next: Next, we put every piece together: a classifier, then a small network, trained from scratch on a spiral of points, one line at a time.
